sections.html: Champaign County covers about 998 square miles of flat farmland and two linked cities, Champaign and Urbana, which nearly wrap around the University of Illinois campus. Urbana is the seat of government. Mid-2025 population is estimated at 209,972, with owners living in 54.0% of homes and a median owned-home value of $211,500. Those numbers describe the whole county, so a farmhouse east of I-57 and a campus-area duplex can look nothing alike on a tax bill. Price from nearby sales, and treat the countywide median as background only.

sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Champaign County
sections.html:
Four county offices split the job. Think of it as value, disputes, money and redemption: one office sets the number, one hears complaints, one sends the bill, and one deals with sold taxes.

  • Supervisor of Assessments: receives the work of the township assessors, mails change notices and processes homestead exemptions. The assessment office number is 217-384-3760.
  • Board of Review: a panel of three, appointed by the County Board once they pass a state exam. They hear complaints, equalize values between townships and add omitted property to the rolls.
  • Treasurer and Collector: sends out about 77,000 real estate bills a year and splits the money among 125 taxing districts. The office number is 217-384-3743.
  • County Clerk: takes redemptions once a tax sale has happened and works out the rates once every taxing body files its levy.

You will find the Treasurer inside the Scott M. Bennett Administrative Center, 102 E. Main Street, Urbana. About 3,400 mobile homes get separate bills, due sixty days after mailing.

Each township assessor values property using a January 1 snapshot, then hands the results to the Supervisor of Assessments by June 15. The target is one-third of market value. When a township's level drifts away from that share, the Supervisor can apply a township multiplier, and those multipliers are published in newspapers and on the county website.

State revenue officials audit the county's assessment work every cycle. If it finds the work properly done, it issues a multiplier of 1.

Schools claim the biggest share. Each taxing body votes a levy by December 31 and sends it to the County Clerk, and state law caps most increases at growth in assessed value and the consumer price index. Mailing finishes by May 1. You owe the tax even if no bill reaches you, so call the Treasurer for another copy.

Expect the bill in early May, with installments typically due in June and September. A postmark on the due date is good enough. Your coupon lists this year's exact dates.

State law adds interest of 1.5% for each month or partial month a payment is late, and each coupon prints a schedule. A payment returned for any reason is void, with a $30 charge plus statutory interest. Personal and business checks work through September 30. After that the counter wants cash, money orders, cashier's checks or certified checks.

  • Use a participating local bank from the list on the county website.
  • Mail the coupon and a check made out to Champaign County Collector to P.O. Box 4306, Springfield, IL 62708-4306.
  • Call 217-834-8713 or go online and use a card or eCheck with the property's PIN. A vendor fee applies.
  • Walk in to 102 E. Main Street, Urbana, weekdays 8 to 4:30, or use the 24-hour drop box in the parking lot.

Your window to complain to the Board of Review runs July 1 through September 10, and hearings happen inside it. Once it closes, members research values and put decisions in writing. The office keeps 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. hours Monday through Thursday, or sees people by appointment.

If you carry the dispute to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, the board speaks for the county there. Back up your number with paper: the closing statement from your purchase and nearby sales of similar homes.

An exemption comes off the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied. The bill drops, and nobody has decided your house is worth less.

Champaign County homeowner exemptions
ExemptionReductionWho qualifies
General homestead (Section 15-175)$6,000Owner's primary residence on January 1 of the assessment year
Senior citizens (Section 15-177)$5,000Owners who turn 65 by the end of the assessment year
Senior assessment freeze (Section 15-172)Holds value at a base yearHousehold income up to $75,000, renewed yearly with proof of income
Persons with disabilities (Section 15-168)$2,000Owners with a qualifying disability
Service-connected disability (Section 15-169)Scaled to the disability rating, up to the full assessed value at 70% or higherOwners with a qualifying service-connected disability

Forms by fax or email are not accepted, so call and ask for a mailed copy. If the house sells, ask whether your exemption ends and what the buyer needs to file.

The house stays yours; the debt is what changes hands. The Collector sends a certified delinquent notice in October and prints the owner's name and amount in the newspaper. Whatever is unpaid after 4:30 p.m. on October 29 goes into the October 30 sale, where an investor pays the tax and gets a claim on the property.

Afterward you owe the sold amount plus interest at the sale-day rate. Roughly two weeks on, the County Clerk (217-384-3722) can give you the redemption figure, and the Clerk's Take Notice follows within four months. You pay the Clerk, who reimburses the investor. The usual period is 3 years from the sale date, with exceptions in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. If nobody redeems, the investor may petition the circuit court for a deed.

Read the closing statement closely. The Treasurer points both sides to the closing papers, the title company or the attorney for any tax owed. Depending on the closing date and when the deed is recorded, the next bill may still go to the previous owner, who has to pass it along.

No bill in hand? Request a duplicate by PIN and check whether either installment is open. When taxes are behind, find out what clearing them costs before closing, because unpaid taxes head toward the October sale. Anything open for the current year gets settled through the title company or attorney.

Have four items ready when you call: the property PIN, the closing date, the expected recording date and the buyer's mailing address. That lets the office say what is paid, what is open and where the next bill goes.

faqs.q: Which office mails Champaign County tax bills?
faqs.a: The County Treasurer, who also acts as Collector, normally mails them in early May. You owe the tax even if a bill goes missing, and 217-384-3743 gets you a duplicate.

faqs.q: What is the Champaign County appeal window?
faqs.a: File with the Board of Review between July 1 and September 10. After that date members research values and issue written decisions.

faqs.q: Are personal checks taken at the counter after September 30?
faqs.a: No. Personal and business checks stop on September 30. From October 1 the counter takes cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks only.

faqs.q: Does a tax sale mean I lose my house?
faqs.a: Not right away. Only the unpaid tax is sold, and you can redeem it through the County Clerk with interest. A court deed comes into play only if the redemption period runs out.

faqs.q: How much is the general homestead exemption in Champaign County?
faqs.a: It is a $6,000 cut in equalized assessed value for an owner-occupied primary residence. Call 217-384-3760 to get the application mailed.
